collection.electronics.entry.bridge_rect: Four diodes combined in one package to turn alternating current into direct current. The tildes mark the AC input, the plus and minus signs the output. It sits at the input of many power supplies.
collection.electronics.entry.ceramic_cap: The humblest of capacitors: it stores a tiny charge and releases it almost at once. It is mostly used to filter out electrical noise. A single circuit board can hold dozens of them.
collection.electronics.entry.coin_cell.d: It powers watches, car keys and small devices for years. In computers, it keeps the time and settings while the machine is off. It is dangerous if swallowed, so it is kept out of children's reach.
collection.electronics.entry.cooling_fan: It moves heat out of computers and power supplies. Dust eventually clogs and wears it down. A fan that starts to rattle or whine is often near the end of its life.
collection.electronics.entry.core_memory: Each magnetic ring stored a single bit. These planes were often woven by hand, wire by wire. This memory, used in computers from the 1950s to the 1970s, kept its data even without power.
collection.electronics.entry.cpu.descrip: The processor carries out a program's instructions: it is the heart of a computer. Its pins are so thin that a single bent one can make it useless. Older models contain a little gold, which interests recyclers.
collection.electronics.entry.cpu.name: processor
collection.electronics.entry.dial_lamp.d: It lit the dials of radios, stereos and dashboards with a warm glow. Its filament always burned out sooner or later. LEDs have replaced it almost everywhere.
collection.electronics.entry.diode.descr: A diode lets current flow in one direction only, like a check valve. The band marks the cathode, the side the current flows out of. It protects circuits from being connected backward.
collection.electronics.entry.diode.name: diode
collection.electronics.entry.electret_mi: A permanently charged membrane picks up vibrations in the air. Small and cheap, it was long used in most phones. It is still found in many headsets and recording devices.
collection.electronics.entry.electrolyti: It holds far more charge than a ceramic capacitor, which makes it the reservoir of power supply circuits. A stripe on its side marks the negative lead, and reversing it can destroy it. With age, it may bulge and leak, giving off a distinctive smell.
collection.electronics.entry.ferrite_cor: Ferrite is a magnetic ceramic that absorbs high-frequency interference. Slipped over a cable, it keeps the cable from acting as an antenna. It is what makes the cylindrical bulge near the plug of many cables.
It sacrifices itself to protect the rest of the circuit: its wire melts if the current gets too high. A blown fuse can be recognized by its broken wire, sometimes by its blackened glass. It must be replaced with one of the same rating, never higher.
collection.electronics.entry.hall_sensor: It detects a magnetic field without any contact. Paired with a small magnet, it lets a laptop know, for example, that its lid is closed. It is also used to measure how fast wheels are turning.
collection.electronics.entry.inductor.de: An inductor resists changes in current by building up a magnetic field. Paired with a capacitor, it forms a circuit that resonates at a precise frequency. This is how radios tune in to a station.
collection.electronics.entry.laser_diode: A diode that emits a tightly focused beam of light. It reads and writes optical discs, and powers laser pointers and barcode scanners. Its beam should never be looked at directly.
collection.electronics.entry.led.descrip: A light-emitting diode produces light when current passes through it. Long limited to red, green and yellow, it only became an efficient blue light in the 1990s. That breakthrough paved the way for the white LEDs that now light our cities.
collection.electronics.entry.led.name: LED
collection.electronics.entry.magic_eye.d: This tuning indicator was fitted to mid-twentieth-century radio sets. Its green glow formed a fan whose shadow narrowed as the dial neared the right station. It gave the set an almost living gaze.
collection.electronics.entry.mercury_swi: As the drop of mercury rolls to one end of the bulb, it closes the contact. Reliable and silent, it was used in many wall thermostats. Its toxicity has led to bans in many countries.
collection.electronics.entry.microcontro: A complete computer on a single chip: processor, memory and inputs and outputs. It runs washing machines, remote controls, toys and countless everyday objects. Billions are made every year.
collection.electronics.entry.neon_indica: Under enough voltage, the neon gas inside glows orange. It showed that a device was switched on, on power strips and irons alike. It uses very little power and lasts a long time.
collection.electronics.entry.nine_volt_b: Inside, several small cells are stacked to add up to nine volts. It powers smoke detectors, effects pedals and test equipment. Many people have tested one with the tip of their tongue and remember the tingle.
Each numeral is an electrode that glows orange when powered. From the 1950s to the 1970s, it displayed numbers on calculators and test equipment. Today it is sought after for building clocks.
collection.electronics.entry.op_amp.desc: It amplifies, compares and combines electrical signals. Its name comes from early analog computers, where it carried out mathematical operations. Today it is found in almost every audio device.
collection.electronics.entry.op_amp.name: operational amplifier
collection.electronics.entry.phone_batte: The lithium-ion battery made modern portable devices possible. It stores a lot of energy for its weight, but handles impacts and heat poorly. Swollen or punctured, it can catch fire.
collection.electronics.entry.photoresist: Its resistance drops as the light increases. It was long used to switch on night-lights and street lighting at dusk. Today it is increasingly replaced by more modern sensors.
collection.electronics.entry.piezo_buzze: Inside, a piezoelectric ceramic flexes under voltage and makes the air vibrate. It is the source of most everyday beeps, from microwave ovens to alarm clocks. It is simple, cheap and uses very little power.
It senses the heat given off by a moving body. Its faceted dome focuses that infrared radiation onto the sensor. It switches on hallway and stairwell lights as people pass, and triggers many alarms.
collection.electronics.entry.potentiomet: A resistor that can be adjusted by hand. It hides behind most volume knobs. As it wears, its track gets dirty and it starts to crackle when turned.
collection.electronics.entry.power_trans: It switches large currents and heats up accordingly. The hole in its tab is for bolting it to a heat sink that carries the heat away. Without one, the component would soon burn out.
collection.electronics.entry.quartz_crys: Inside, a sliver of quartz crystal vibrates at a highly stable frequency. That vibration serves as a time reference for watches, clocks and computers. The one in a watch beats 32,768 times per second.
A computer's working memory, fast but volatile: it forgets everything as soon as the power is cut. The earliest modules held only a few megabytes. Their gold contacts resist corrosion.
collection.electronics.entry.relay.descr: A switch controlled by another current: an electromagnet pulls the strip, and the contact closes with a sharp click. Early automatic telephone exchanges held thousands of them. They are still found in cars and electrical panels.
collection.electronics.entry.relay.name: relay
collection.electronics.entry.resistor.de: A resistor limits the flow of current. Its colored bands form a code that gives its value, which electronics hobbyists often memorize with mnemonic phrases. It is one of the most common components there is.
collection.electronics.entry.rotary_swit: It selects between several circuits, one notch at a time. It is found on multimeters, old radio sets and washing machines. Each notch connects a different contact.
collection.electronics.entry.sim_card.de: It identifies a subscriber on the mobile network. Its clipped corner keeps it from being inserted the wrong way. Over the generations it has kept shrinking, to the point of disappearing entirely from some phones.
collection.electronics.entry.small_speak: A coil placed near a magnet makes the cone vibrate in time with the signal. The principle has barely changed since the 1920s. This one probably came from a toy or a pocket radio.
collection.electronics.entry.small_trans: It steps mains voltage down to a level devices can use. Its plates vibrate slightly in time with the alternating current. That is the hum heard in old chargers and power supplies.
It converts light directly into electricity. The thin silver lines collect the current generated on its surface. Pocket calculators had small ones that worked even under a desk lamp.
collection.electronics.entry.stepper_mot: It turns in precise steps rather than continuously, which allows a mechanism to be positioned without a sensor. Printers, scanners and 3D printers owe their exact movements to it. It also produces their distinctive mechanical whine.
collection.electronics.entry.supercapaci: It stores hundreds of times more energy than a standard capacitor and releases it very quickly. It recharges in seconds and withstands hundreds of thousands of cycles. It is used to keep memory alive or to deliver bursts of power.
A resistor whose value changes sharply with temperature. It monitors the heat of batteries, ovens and water heaters. Digital thermometers often contain one.
collection.electronics.entry.tilt_switch: Depending on the tilt, the ball opens or closes the contact. This simple principle detects that an object has been moved or knocked over. They are found in toys, alarms and some heaters.
collection.electronics.entry.timer_555.d: Designed in the early 1970s, it is among the most widely produced integrated circuits in history. It is used to generate pulses, blinking lights or tones. Generations of hobbyists built their first circuits with it.
collection.electronics.entry.toggle_swit: The switch at its simplest: one lever, two positions. It is found on dashboards, amplifiers and cockpits. Its position can be read by touch, without looking.
A transistor lets a small current control a larger one, like a faucet. Invented in 1947, it replaced vacuum tubes in most devices. Modern chips contain billions of them.
collection.electronics.entry.uv_eprom.de: A memory chip that kept its data without power and was erased by shining ultraviolet light through its quartz window. The window was covered with a label, since daylight could slowly erase it. It was replaced by flash memory.
collection.electronics.entry.vacuum_tube: Before the transistor, it amplified and switched electrical signals. Radios had to warm up before working, while its filaments came to a glow. It is still sought after for guitar amplifiers and high-end audio.
collection.electronics.entry.variable_ca: Changing how much the plates overlap changes its capacitance. Linked to the tuning knob, it let old radios tune in to a station. Modern receivers have replaced it with electronic circuits.
collection.electronics.entry.vibration_m: As it spins, its unbalanced weight shakes the whole device. It is what makes phones and game controllers vibrate. Recent models have often replaced it with a more precise actuator.
collection.electronics.name: electronic components
collection.minerals.entry.agate.descript: It forms inside cavities in volcanic rock, layer by layer, like the rings of a tree. Each band marks a deposit of silica. Its hardness made it a material for mortars and marbles.
collection.minerals.entry.agate.name: agate
collection.minerals.entry.alexandrite.de: A rare variety of chrysoberyl, discovered in the Ural Mountains in the nineteenth century. It looks green in daylight and red under an incandescent bulb. This change of color makes it one of the most sought-after gems.
collection.minerals.entry.amber.descript: Fossilized tree resin, millions of years old. It sometimes holds insects trapped intact. When rubbed, it attracts dust: its Greek name, elektron, gave us the word electricity.
collection.minerals.entry.amber.name: amber
collection.minerals.entry.amethyst.descr: A purple quartz, colored by traces of iron and natural radioactivity. Its Greek name means “not drunk,” as it was believed to protect against intoxication. When heated, it turns yellow.
collection.minerals.entry.amethyst.name: amethyst
collection.minerals.entry.ammonite.descr: A marine mollusk related to the octopus, which lived in a coiled shell. Ammonites filled the seas for more than three hundred million years. They died out at the same time as the dinosaurs.
collection.minerals.entry.ammonite.name: ammonite
collection.minerals.entry.basalt.descrip: Lava that cooled quickly in the open air. As it contracts, it sometimes forms tall six-sided columns. The ocean floor is made almost entirely of it.
collection.minerals.entry.basalt.name: basalt
collection.minerals.entry.bauxite.descri: The ore from which aluminum is made. It is named after the village of Les Baux-de-Provence, where it was identified in the nineteenth century. Turning bauxite into metal takes enormous amounts of electricity.
collection.minerals.entry.bauxite.name: bauxite
collection.minerals.entry.calcite.descri: The mineral that makes up limestone, marble and seashells. Its clearest variety splits any image seen through it in two. It also forms the stalactites and stalagmites of caves.
collection.minerals.entry.calcite.name: calcite
collection.minerals.entry.cassiterite.de: The main ore of tin. Alloyed with copper, tin makes bronze, which gave its name to an entire age of human history. It is very dense and builds up in river sands.
collection.minerals.entry.chalcopyrite.d: The most common copper ore in the world. Exposed to air, its surface tarnishes to a rainbow-colored film. Like pyrite, it has often been mistaken for gold.
collection.minerals.entry.cinnabar.descr: The ore of mercury. Ground up, it made vermilion, a brilliant red prized by painters and lacquer makers. It is toxic, and should only be handled with care.
collection.minerals.entry.cinnabar.name: cinnabar
collection.minerals.entry.emerald.descri: A beryl colored green by traces of chromium or vanadium. Its inclusions are so common that they are nicknamed its “garden.” A flawless emerald is extremely rare.
collection.minerals.entry.emerald.name: emerald
collection.minerals.entry.fern_fossil.de: The imprint of a fern from the swamp forests of three hundred million years ago. Those forests, buried and compressed, formed much of today's coal. Such fossils are often found in old coal mines.
collection.minerals.entry.flint.descript: A very hard rock made of silica, which forms as nodules within chalk. It breaks into razor-sharp flakes, which made it the material of the earliest tools. Struck against steel, it throws sparks.
collection.minerals.entry.flint.name: flint
collection.minerals.entry.fluorite.descr: A mineral found in many colors, from purple to green to yellow. It gave its name to fluorescence, because some specimens glow under ultraviolet light. It is also used in steelmaking and optical lenses.
collection.minerals.entry.fluorite.name: fluorite
collection.minerals.entry.fossil_egg.des: A dinosaur egg, turned to stone over millions of years. Some still contain the bones of an embryo. The south of France has some major deposits of them.
collection.minerals.entry.fulgurite.desc: The path of a lightning bolt frozen in the ground. When lightning strikes sand, it melts it in an instant, leaving a hollow tube of glass. Some fulgurites reach several meters deep.
collection.minerals.entry.fulgurite.name: fulgurite
collection.minerals.entry.galena.descrip: The main ore of lead, which breaks into perfect little cubes. In the early twentieth century, a single galena crystal was enough to pick up radio broadcasts: these were crystal sets. It often contains a little silver.
collection.minerals.entry.galena.name: galena
collection.minerals.entry.garnet.descrip: A family of minerals whose crystals resemble pomegranate seeds, hence their name. Being very hard, they are also used as an abrasive in sandpaper. Dark red is their best-known color, but they come in almost every shade.
collection.minerals.entry.garnet.name: garnet
collection.minerals.entry.geode.descript: A cavity in rock where mineral-rich water deposited crystals over thousands of years. From the outside, nothing sets it apart from an ordinary stone. It has to be broken open to discover what it holds.
collection.minerals.entry.geode.name: geode
collection.minerals.entry.gold_nugget.de: Gold neither rusts nor tarnishes, which made it a symbol of permanence. It is so malleable that it can be beaten into sheets thinner than a hair. Nuggets are mostly found in riverbeds.
collection.minerals.entry.granite.descri: It forms from magma that cooled slowly, far below the surface. Its speckles are three distinct minerals: quartz, feldspar and mica. Its hardness makes it a stone of choice for monuments and countertops.
collection.minerals.entry.granite.name: granite
collection.minerals.entry.gypsum.descrip: Heated and ground, it becomes plaster. The gypsum mined beneath the hill of Montmartre was so renowned that the name “plaster of Paris” is still used. In the desert, it sometimes forms petal-shaped crystals known as desert roses.
collection.minerals.entry.gypsum.name: gypsum
collection.minerals.entry.halite.descrip: Ordinary salt, left behind by the evaporation of ancient seas. Its crystals form near-perfect cubes. Salt was once so valuable that it served as currency, and the word salary comes from it.
collection.minerals.entry.halite.name: rock salt
collection.minerals.entry.hematite.descr: The main ore of iron. Although it is gray, its powder is blood red, hence its name, from the Greek word for blood. Ground up, it served as a pigment for prehistoric cave painters.
collection.minerals.entry.hematite.name: hematite
collection.minerals.entry.iron_meteorite: A fragment of an asteroid's core, made of iron and nickel, that fell from the sky. The hollows on its surface were carved by the heat of its passage through the atmosphere. Cut and polished, it reveals a crisscross pattern of crystals found in no rock on Earth.
collection.minerals.entry.jasper.descrip: An opaque form of silica, colored by iron oxides. Seals, beads and amulets were made from it in ancient times. Its patterns vary so much that no two stones look alike.
collection.minerals.entry.jasper.name: jasper
collection.minerals.entry.lapis_lazuli.d: A blue rock whose golden flecks are pyrite. Ground up, it made ultramarine, a pigment that long cost more than gold. Painters often reserved it for the robes of the most important figures.
collection.minerals.entry.limestone.desc: A sedimentary rock formed largely from the remains of marine organisms. Much of Paris was built from limestone quarried beneath its streets. A drop of vinegar is enough to make it fizz.
collection.minerals.entry.limestone.name: limestone
collection.minerals.entry.magnetite.desc: The most magnetic mineral in nature. Some naturally magnetized pieces were used to make the first compasses. Some birds and bacteria contain tiny crystals of it, which may help them find their way.
collection.minerals.entry.magnetite.name: magnetite
collection.minerals.entry.malachite.desc: A copper mineral that forms when the metal weathers near the surface. Ground up, it long served as a green pigment. Some palaces decorated entire rooms with it.
collection.minerals.entry.malachite.name: malachite
collection.minerals.entry.mica.descripti: A mineral that splits into flexible, transparent sheets. It withstands heat and does not conduct electricity. It was used for stove windows and as insulation in early electrical devices.
collection.minerals.entry.mica.name: mica
Almost pure copper, just as nature laid it down. It is one of the first metals humans ever worked, more than ten thousand years ago. Over time, it acquires a green patina.
Pure silver sometimes forms as twisted wires sprouting from the rock. In contact with air, it slowly tarnishes black. It conducts electricity better than any other metal.
collection.minerals.entry.obsidian.descr: A volcanic glass, formed when lava cooled too quickly to crystallize. Its flakes are sharper than a steel blade. Many peoples made arrowheads, knives and mirrors from it.
collection.minerals.entry.obsidian.name: obsidian
collection.minerals.entry.opal.descripti: A form of silica that contains water, made of tiny stacked spheres. These spheres break light into flashes of color. It can crack if it dries out.
collection.minerals.entry.opal.name: opal
collection.minerals.entry.platinum_nugge: Rarer than gold, platinum resists corrosion and extreme heat. The conquistadors thought it worthless and called it “little silver.” Today it is found in catalytic converters and jewelry.
collection.minerals.entry.pumice.descrip: Lava so full of gas that it froze like foam. Its bubbles are so numerous that it floats on water. It has been used to polish and smooth surfaces since ancient times.
collection.minerals.entry.pumice.name: pumice
collection.minerals.entry.pyrite.descrip: An iron sulfide nicknamed “fool's gold,” since many have mistaken it for gold. Its name comes from the Greek word for fire: struck against steel, it throws sparks. Its crystals often grow as near-perfect cubes.
collection.minerals.entry.pyrite.name: pyrite
collection.minerals.entry.quartz.descrip: Pure quartz, one of the most common minerals in the Earth's crust. Under pressure, it produces a small electric charge, which makes it essential to watches and electronic clocks. The ancients believed it was ice that would never melt.
collection.minerals.entry.quartz.name: rock crystal
collection.minerals.entry.rose_quartz.de: A variety of quartz tinted by tiny traces of other minerals. It rarely forms distinct crystals and is usually found in masses. Its color fades if it is left in the sun for long.
Pure carbon, crystallized under immense pressure more than a hundred kilometers underground. It is the hardest natural material, yet the same element as pencil lead. In the rough, it barely shines: cutting is what reveals its brilliance.
collection.minerals.entry.ruby.descripti: A corundum, colored red by traces of chromium. It is the same mineral as sapphire: only the color sets them apart. The first laser, built in 1960, ran on a ruby crystal.
collection.minerals.entry.ruby.name: ruby
collection.minerals.entry.sandstone.desc: Grains of sand bound together by a natural cement. Very hard-wearing, it was long used to cut paving stones for city streets. Its rough surface also made it a sharpening stone.
collection.minerals.entry.sandstone.name: sandstone
collection.minerals.entry.sapphire.descr: A corundum, like ruby: every corundum that is not red is a sapphire, even yellow or pink ones. After diamond, it is one of the hardest natural materials. Synthetic sapphire protects the face of many watches.
collection.minerals.entry.sapphire.name: sapphire
collection.minerals.entry.shark_tooth.de: A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage, which very rarely fossilizes. Their teeth, on the other hand, are well preserved, and a shark sheds thousands of them in its lifetime. They were long believed to be petrified snake tongues.
collection.minerals.entry.slate.descript: A metamorphic rock formed from clay that was compressed and heated deep underground. It splits into thin, waterproof sheets, hence its use for roofing. Schoolchildren once wrote on it with chalk.
collection.minerals.entry.slate.name: slate
collection.minerals.entry.sulfur.descrip: It forms around the vents of volcanoes. Odorless when pure, it gives off a choking smell when it burns. Its crystals are so sensitive to heat that they can crackle in the palm of a hand.
collection.minerals.entry.sulfur.name: sulfur
collection.minerals.entry.talc.descripti: The softest of all minerals: a fingernail is enough to scratch it. Ground to powder, it soothes the skin and absorbs moisture. As soapstone, it has been carved for thousands of years.
collection.minerals.entry.talc.name: talc
collection.minerals.entry.tigers_eye.des: A quartz that replaced an older mineral, fiber by fiber. Those fibers reflect light as a shifting band, an effect called chatoyancy. It was once worn as protection against the evil eye.
collection.minerals.entry.trilobite.desc: A marine arthropod that lived for nearly three hundred million years, long before the dinosaurs. Its eyes were made of calcite crystals, among the oldest known eyes. It vanished in the greatest extinction in Earth's history.
collection.minerals.entry.trilobite.name: trilobite
collection.minerals.entry.turquoise.desc: A phosphate of copper and aluminum, one of the first ornamental stones ever mined. Its name comes from the fact that it reached Europe by way of Turkey. It is sensitive to heat, oils and perfume.
collection.minerals.entry.turquoise.name: turquoise
